abstract:
Consumption of bioactive milk proteins enhances preterm
infant
development. Preterm infants are often supplemented with donor human
milk (DHM) when parents’ own milk is unavailable in sufficient
quantity. DHM is normally Holder pasteurized (HoP) to inactivate pathogens;
however, it denatures many bioactive proteins. Alternatively, ultraviolet-C
(UV–C) irradiation can inactivate pathogens while preserving
milk proteins. This study examined the effects of HoP and UV–C
on the proteome of DHM ( n = 1 pool, processing in
triplicate). Protein counts in HoP samples ( n = 198)
were lower than in raw DHM ( n = 228) and UV–C
at 6000 J/L ( n = 239) samples. HoP resulted in significant
reductions in relative abundance for 80 proteins ( p -values <0.05, >0.5-fold decrease), whereas UV–C at
6000
J/L resulted in only 5 proteins significantly decreasing. Proteins
reduced by HoP that were preserved by UV–C treatment had a
broad array of functions, including antimicrobial, iron-binding, immunomodulatory,
and proteolytic. Applying UV–C processing for donor milk processing
could improve outcomes in preterm infants.

Materials and Methods
2.1
DHM Collection and Milk Processing
A pool of DHM was collected and donated by the Northwest Mothers
Milk Bank (Tigard, OR). The pooled DHM was aliquoted from one pool
(
n
= 1) into 50 mL tubes and stored at −20
°C until additional treatment.
Before DHM treatments, aliquots
of frozen, pooled DHM were thawed at 4 °C overnight. To create
raw DHM samples (referred to as “Raw”), the thawed DHM
was aliquoted into three separate 1.5 mL tubes and stored at −80
°C immediately, and further sample preparation and analyses were
performed independently on the three raw samples as described below
(
n
= 3 processing replicates). HoP and UV–C
treatment were performed as described previously
and independently repeated in triplicate. Briefly, HoP
was performed by placing 5 mL of DHM in 15 mL tubes into a water bath
at 62.5 °C, measuring sample temperature until it reached 62.5
°C, and further incubating for 30 min (
n
= 3
processing replicates; referred to as “HoP”). After
thermal processing, HoP-treated samples were immediately placed in
an ice bath, aliquoted to 1.5 mL tubes, and stored at −80 °C.
For the UV–C processing, 120 mL of DHM were treated using the
UV–C lamp described previously,
and 1 mL of the milk was collected every 2 min (1000 J/L interval)
from 4 to 22 min (from 2000 to 11,000 J/L; referred to as “UV–C”)
in 1.5 mL tubes (
n
= 3 processing replicates for
each UV–C dose). Upon collection of each sample, tubes were
immediately placed in an ice bath, and all tubes were stored at −80
°C upon treatment completion. We included a broad range of UV–C
doses to enable examination of the impact of dose on the DHM proteome.
Among these, for comparisons with HoP, which provides >5-log reductions
of vegetative bacteria, we focused on one specific dose, 6000 J/L,
which we have previously demonstrated to provide >5-log reductions
of vegetative bacteria (
C. sakazakii
,
L. monocytogenes
, and
E. faecium
).
During
UV–C processing, the temperature of DHM was measured using
a liquid-in-glass thermometer. During UV–C treatment, measured
inner temperatures of human milk were on average between 14.3 °C
at 2000 J/L of UV–C dose and 22.5 °C at 11,000 J/L (
Supporting Table 1
).
2.2
Intact Soluble Human Milk Protein Extraction
Raw and treated DHM samples (500 μL each) were thawed at
4 °C and centrifuged at 12,000
g
at 4 °C
for 10 min, and 200 μL of infranatant (between the upper lipid
layer and lower pellet) was collected into a new tube. In these collected
samples, 0.1 M HCl (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany) was added until a pH
of 4.6 was achieved to precipitate insoluble proteins, including caseins
and other aggregates. pH-adjusted samples were centrifuged at 4 °C
for 30 min at 4000
g
, based on a previous method.
One hundred microliters of each second infranatant
(between the minor residual lipid layer and precipitated protein layer)
were collected into a new tube. To extract the intact proteins from
the endogenous peptides in DHM, samples were filtered by 10-kDa molecular
weight cutoff filtration as described previously.
Briefly, a centrifugal filtration device was cleaned with
ultrapure water (18.2 MW·cm), and samples were loaded in the
filter and washed with ultrapure water (500 μL). The retentate
containing human milk proteins was transferred to a collection tube.
2.3
Trypsin Digestion of Intact Human Milk Proteins
Each retentate sample (∼30 μL) was mixed with 100
μL of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate (Thermo Scientific, Waltham,
MA) followed by 2 μL of 550 mM dithiothreitol (Promega, Madison,
WI). Samples were then incubated at 50 °C for 50 min to reduce
the number of disulfide bonds. After incubation, 4 μL of 450
mM iodoacetamide (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO) was added and incubated
at room temperature (20–23 °C) for 60 min in the dark
to alkylate the thiol groups. Then, 3 μL of trypsin/Lys-C (1
μg/μL, Promega) were added to each sample and incubated
at 37 °C overnight with shaking at 300 rpm in a thermomixer.
2.4
Enrichment and Purification of Tryptic Peptides
Tryptic peptides were enriched and purified by solid-phase extraction
using C18 96-well plates (1 mL tube volume, 50 mg bed weight, and
45 μm particle size; Biotage, Uppsala, Sweden). C18 96-well
plates were washed with 900 μL (3 × 300 μL) of ultrapure
water, followed by 900 μL (3 × 300 μL) of elution
solvent containing 80% acetonitrile (ACN; Merck, Darmstadt, Germany)
and 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid (Merck). The 96-well plates were reconditioned
with 900 μL (3 × 300 μL) of ultrapure water prior
to loading the samples. Samples were loaded on the plates and washed
with 900 μL (300 μL × 3 times) of ultrapure water
to remove salts and interfering substances. Nine hundred microliters
(300 μL × 3 times) of elution solvent were added to elute
the tryptic peptides from the C18 96-well plates. All of the eluates
were completely dried via vacuum centrifugation.
2.5
LC/MS and MS/MS Analysis of DHM Protein-Derived
Tryptic Peptides
Tryptic peptides were analyzed using a Waters
nanoACQUITY UPLC instrument (Waters, Milford, MA) with an Orbitrap
Fusion Lumos Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, Waltham,
MA). Dried samples were reconstituted with 100 μL of 3% ACN
and 0.1% formic acid (Sigma-Aldrich) and diluted 2.5-fold. One microliter
of each sample was loaded onto a C18 180 μm × 20 mm, 5
μm bead nanoAcquity UPLC trap column (Waters) for enrichment
and desalting, and separated with a 100 μm × 100 mm, 1.7
μm bead Acquity UPLC Peptide BEH C18 column (Waters) over 60
min. Peptides were separated at a flow rate of 0.5 μL/min with
a gradient elution using solvent A (ultrapure water with 0.1% formic
acid) and solvent B (ACN with 0.1% formic acid): 3–11.5% B,
0–10 min; 11.5–20% B, 10–31 min; 20–30%
B, 31–36 min; 30–95% B, 36–45 min; 95% B, 45–54.5
min; 95–3% B over 0.5 min. Then, the column was re-equilibrated
with 97% A for 5 min.
Tryptic peptides were ionized with an
electrospray voltage of 2350 V and an ion transfer tube temperature
of 300 °C. Full scan MS spectra were acquired in positive ionization
mode over an
m
/
z
range of 300–2000
with a resolution of 60,000. The automatic gain control target was
set to 4.0 × 10
5
, with a maximum injection time of
50 ms. The MS cycle time was set to 3 s. Following an MS scan, acquisition
software automatically selected precursor compounds for MS/MS analysis
based on the following criteria: ion intensity threshold 5.0 ×
10
4
, charge state 2–8, and exclusion time 60 s.
Higher energy collision dissociation-based fragmentation was performed
with 30% collision energy. All MS/MS spectra were acquired in the
positive ionization and auto scan range modes by the Orbitrap at a
resolution of 60,000. The automatic gain control target was set to
5.0 × 10
4
.
2.6
Data Processing and Statistical Analysis
The tryptic peptides from raw files were processed using Proteome
Discoverer (v.3.1; Thermo Scientific) with the Sequest HT search engine
against an in-house human milk protein sequence database (
n
= 382). Cleavage sites were set to C-terminal arginine
(R) and lysine (K), and digestion specificity was selected as fully
specific with a maximum of two missed cleavages. The precursor mass
tolerance was set to 10 ppm with fragment mass tolerance of 0.1 Da.
Minimum and maximum peptide length were set to 4 and 160 amino acids,
respectively. Potential modifications included phosphorylation (+79.966
Da) of serine and threonine, oxidation (+15.995 Da) of methionine,
and acetylation (+42.011 Da) of the N-terminus. Carbamidomethylation
(+57.021 Da) of cysteine was specified as a fixed modification. Only
proteins identified with high confidence (
q
-value
<0.01) were retained for further analysis.
The total protein
count, indicating the number of proteins identified in each sample
type, was obtained from the Proteome Discoverer. The abundances of
each identified protein were measured by using the sum of the area
under the curve of the extracted ion chromatograms of the matched
peptides. Abundances of proteins in experimental triplicates were
averaged and expressed as mean values ± the standard error of
the mean.
Pearson correlation analysis (
R
)
was conducted
to compare the abundance of proteins that were identical across different
sample types (Raw, HoP, and UV–C) and experimental and instrument
replicates by data analysis in Excel. The similarities and differences
in proteins among the samples were assessed via one-way ANOVA and
Tukey’s post hoc test (
p
-value <0.05) using
SPSS Statistics for Windows (v.18.0; SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL). Differing
letters on the bar graphs indicate statistical differences. Principal
component analysis (PCA) 2D plots, volcano plots, and heat maps were
generated using Excel and web-enabled tools (MetaboAnalyst 6.0, VolcaNoseR,
and Heatmapper) as described previously.
A gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis was conducted using
the
PANTHER classification system (
https://pantherdb.org/
) to assess protein function and subcellular
origin of proteins that significantly changed after treatment. Hydrophobicity
of the human milk proteins was investigated using the web-enabled
tool, GRAVY Calculator (
https://www.gravy-calculator.de/
).

1
Introduction
Approximately 10% of infants
are born preterm (<37 weeks of
gestation). These infants experience less in utero physiological development
than term infants, rendering them vulnerable to poor growth, increased
risk for gastrointestinal diseases and infections, and poor neurological
development compared with term infants.
,
Feeding preterm
infants human milk reduces the risk of several morbidities, as compared
with formula feeding, including necrotizing enterocolitis,
,
sepsis,
abnormal brain development,
neonatal chronic lung disease, retinopathy of
prematurity, and features predictive of metabolic syndrome.
Therefore, the American Academy of Pediatrics
recommends that preterm infants be fed with parents’ own milk
or pasteurized donor human milk (DHM) if parents’ milk is not
available in sufficient quantity.
Human milk’s ability to reduce infant disease risk derives
from its functional components. Human milk contains a complex array
of hundreds of proteins with both known and unknown functions that
impact infant health.
−
Known functions include enhancing mineral absorption
(e.g., lactoferrin
and α-lactalbumin
), controlling nutrient absorption (e.g., bile
salt-stimulated lipase (BSSL)
and milk
proteases
,
), defending against bacterial and viral
pathogens (e.g., lactoferrin,
,
lysozyme,
and lactoperoxidase
), preventing adhesion of pathogens to intestinal cells to reduce
infection risk (e.g., immunoglobulins
and mucin
), modulating the immune system
(e.g., cytokines
and osteopontin
), managing oxidative stress (e.g., glutathione
peroxidase, glutathione reductase, and superoxide dismutase
,
) and guiding optimal development of the gastrointestinal system
(e.g., epidermal growth factor,
insulin-like
growth factor (IGF)-1,
and transforming
growth factor β
).
Though
parents’ own milk is preferred for preterm infants,
the majority of lactating parents of preterm infants are unable to
provide an adequate supply of milk (due to physiological factors,
stress, etc.), making supplementation necessary.
Hill et al. demonstrated that 52% of lactating parents
of preterm infants who planned to exclusively feed their own milk
produced inadequate volumes (<500 mL/d) by 6 weeks postpartum.
Therefore, preterm infants are often fed DHM
during their hospitalization, as it also results in improved infant
health outcomes as compared to formula.
Bacterial and viral pathogens can be present in raw DHM, from
either
the lactating parent (mammary gland or skin) or environmental contamination
(pumps, bottles, etc.). To decrease infection risk, nonprofit milk
banks apply Holder pasteurization (62.5 °C, 30 min; HoP) to DHM
to reduce milk vegetative bacterial (by ≥5-log CFU/mL) and
viral (by at least several logs for most viruses studied) loads.
Unfortunately, our group and others have demonstrated
that HoP completely or partially inactivates many bioactive milk proteins,
including digestive enzymes (e.g., BSSL,
elastase
and cathepsin D
), antimicrobial proteins (lactoferrin,
immunoglobulin A (IgA),
IgG,
IgM
and lysozyme
), antioxidant enzymes
(e.g., glutathione peroxidase macrophage inflammatory protein-1β,
Interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α
), growth factors (e.g., IGF-1, IGF-2, insulin-like growth
factor binding protein (IGFBP)-2, IGFBP-3,
erythropoietin,
heparin-binding epidermal-like
growth factor and hepatocyte growth factor
) and hormones (e.g., insulin and adiponectin
).
The degradation of bioactive proteins by HoP could
play a role
(among other factors) in the observed differences in the protective
impact of DHM compared with the parent’s own milk. For example,
infants fed Holder pasteurized parents’ own milk had less lipid
absorption and knee-heel length gain than infants fed unheated parents’
own milk.
Similarly, infants fed Holder
pasteurized DHM had less growth, decreased gut microbial diversity,
and lower rates of neurocognitive development than infants fed their
parents’ own unpasteurized milk.
,
The degradation
of bioactive proteins by HoP is likely partially responsible for the
observed poorer health outcomes for infants fed Holder pasteurized
DHM compared with unheated parents’ own milk. For example,
as human milk BSSL enhances lipid digestion in infants, the loss of
human milk’s BSSL from HoP likely contributes to the observed
poorer lipid absorption and linear growth in preterm infants fed Holder
pasteurized milk compared with those fed untreated human milk.
Ultraviolet (UV)-C irradiation is a potential
nonthermal alternative
to HoP for treating DHM. Ultraviolet-C treatment inactivates pathogens
because the radiation is absorbed by the pyrimidine and purine bases
of DNA and RNA in bacteria and viruses (∼240 to 275 nm), which
causes DNA/RNA cross-linking and disrupts DNA transcription and RNA
translation.
Previous research
studies applied UV–C treatment to human
milk by immersing a UV–C lamp into a beaker of human milk with
continual stirring.
,
Using a lamp immersion setup,
a 6000 J/L UV–C dose allowed a ≥ 5-log reduction of
the vegetative bacteria
Cronobacter sakazakii
,
Listeria monocytogenes
,
Enterococcus faecium
, and
Staphylococcus
aureus
.
No increase in
lipid oxidation products was found (measured as malondialdehyde),
and similar levels of vitamin E were measured after UV–C processing
compared with raw milk.
UV–C treatment
at 6000 J/L also better preserved IgA, IgG, IgM, cathepsin D, elastase,
and lactoferrin (measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA))
and lysozyme and BSSL (measured by activity assays) compared with
HoP. These results align with those of another study that used a UV–C
lamp immersion system and observed ≥5-log reductions of vegetative
bacteria with a >4863 J/L dose and to improved preservation of
IgA,
lactoferrin, lysozyme, and BSSL compared with HoP.
Though several studies have monitored the capacity
of UV–C
treatment to inactivate microbes and preserve specific proteins (via
techniques like ELISA and activity assays) in DHM, only a single previous
study examined the impact of UV–C treatment on a broader array
of proteins by examining the human milk proteome.
This foundational study detected improved retention of
IgA, lactoferrin, lysozyme and other bioactive proteins in UV–C-treated
DHM compared to HoP-treated DHM and that the overall protein profile
after UV–C treatment was more similar to untreated milk than
HoP-treated milk.
The UV–C doses
used in that study were lower than the 6000 J/L we previously determined
as necessary for a >5-log reduction of pathogenic bacteria,
necessitating examination of the proteome impacts
at this higher dose. The previous study also did not provide a list
of all of the proteins significantly changed between raw milk and
HoP and between raw milk and UV–C. No previous study has examined
the extent to which the chemical and physical properties of human
milk proteins affect their stability across HoP and UV–C treatment.
There is a need for additional studies to examine the effects of UV–C
treatment of human milk on the broad array of milk proteins and their
potential functional impacts.
Therefore, our objective herein
is to examine the impacts of UV–C
treatment on the overall human milk proteome in comparison with HoP.
This work is significant, as it will help guide the processing of
DHM to optimize infant health outcomes.

Results and Discussion
3.1
Reproducibility of Replicates
Reproducibility
of the experimental and instrumental replications was investigated
to assess the effects of variation across sample preparation and LC-MS
analysis. Similarity of the proteomics results of Raw replicates (
n
= 3 processing replicates) was evaluated using correlation
analysis and visualized via scatter plotting. The overall data for
protein abundances among Raw processing triplicates were highly correlated
(0.997 <
R
< 0.998;
Supporting Figure 1a
). This finding indicates that there is little impact
of possible variation in sample handling, extraction, and analysis
on the protein profile. To evaluate the possible impact of instrument
variations during operating LC-MS for the large sample set on the
proteomics results, one raw sample processing replicate was analyzed
at 1, 2.5, 5, and 7 days of the LC-MS analysis (across the same period
of analysis for the overall sample set). Measurements of the same
raw sample on different days (1, 2.5, 5, and 7 days) were significantly
correlated (0.997 <
R
< 0.998;
Supporting Figure 1b
). These findings indicate
that there was little day-to-day variation in instrument performance,
enabling further examination of the impacts of heat and UV–C
treatments across the entire sample set.
3.2
Comparison of the Effect of HoP and UV–C
on DHM Proteins
A previous study revealed that 5-log reductions
of vegetative bacteria (
C. sakazakii
,
L. monocytogenes
, and
E. faecium
) were observed in the DHM samples treated
by >6000 J/L of UV–C treatments.
In the current study, DHM samples treated using UV–C at 6000
J/L were compared with the Raw and HoP samples to evaluate the effect
of the HoP and UV–C treatment on DHM proteins.
Protein
counts identified in Raw, HoP, and UV–C at 6000 J/L were 228,
198, and 239, respectively (protein list in
Supporting Table 2
). HoP samples showed relatively lower protein count
compared to Raw and UV–C at 6000 J/L samples. Out of the proteins

To assess the functional
importance of proteins that significantly decreased in abundance (including
those present in Raw but undetectable after treatment), GO enrichment
analysis was performed via the PANTHER classification system, examining
protein function. Those proteins in HoP and UV–C samples were
annotated with 17 and 6 terms, respectively, which were categorized
into two groups: molecular function and biological process (
Figure
and
Supporting Table 6
).

Within the “molecular function” classification
group,
proteins decreased by HoP were mainly involved in “catalytic

Within the “biological process” category, the proteins
that were decreased by HoP included those mainly involved in cellular

(2 proteins, 40%), cellular processes (1 protein, 20%), response to
stimulus (1 protein, 20%), and immune system processes (1 protein,
20%). Thus, these GO analysis results indicated that UV–C treatment
appears to exhibit a minimal effect on the bioactivity of human milk
proteins as compared to HoP treatment.
Among the bioactive proteins
that were significantly reduced after
HoP but not by UV–C (based on volcano plots and GO analysis)
were lactoferrin, BSSL, lactoperoxidase, osteopontin, immunoglobulins
(IgG, IgK and immunoglobulin heavy variable region), macrophage mannose
receptor 1, xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase, retinoid-inducible serine
carboxypeptidase, cathepsin D, cellular retinoic acid-binding protein
2, monocyte differentiation antigen CD14, and peroxiredoxin-6.
Some of the proteins better preserved by UV–C than HoP have
the capacity to modulate the infant microbiome. Lactoferrin (
P02788
)
inhibits the growth of bacteria, viruses, and other pathogens by binding
to iron
,
,
,
or acting as a direct antimicrobial. Lactoperoxidase
(
P22079
) catalyzes the oxidation of thiocyanate ions by hydrogen peroxide,
generating antimicrobial compounds such as hypothiocyanite, and these
oxidation products protect the infant’s digestive tract and
the mammary gland against bacterial infection by inhibiting microbial
growth.
,
,
Xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase
(
P47989
) can generate reactive oxygen and reactive nitrogen species
and act as an antimicrobial.
,
Other proteins
identified as being preserved by UV–C but
not HoP can impact milk digestion and nutrient utilization in the
infant. BSSL (
P19835
) releases free fatty acids from milk triglycerides,
improving nutrient absorption and growth in infants.
,
Retinoid-inducible serine carboxypeptidase (
Q9HB40
) and cathepsin
D (
P07339
) could help control the degradation and utilization of milk
proteins and the release of bioactive peptides in the infant.
,
UV–C at 6000 J/L led to improved preservation of proteins
involved in immunomodulation compared with HoP. Milk osteopontin (
P10451
)
may help regulate the infant’s immune system
,
and enhance intestinal barrier protection.
,
Immunoglobulins play a critical role in transferring immunity from
the lactating parent to the infant, including helping to prevent bacterial
and viral infections through antigen–antibody interactions.
,
CD14 (
P08571
) can exist either as a glycolipid-anchored membrane
glycoprotein on macrophages and dendritic cells (monocyte differentiation
antigen CD14) or as a soluble protein (soluble CD14 (sCD14)) in body
fluids. The observed CD14 herein is likely a sCD14. In fluid, sCD14
can bind to and sequester lipopolysaccharide from bacteria, preventing
inflammation, and in milk, it may help influence which microbes persist
in the gut of infants.
−
Peroxiredoxin-6 (
P30041
) is involved in cell protection
against oxidative stress and cellular senescence and in cellular redox
homeostasis.
,
Macrophage mannose receptor 1
(
P22897
), expressed by macrophages, recognizes mannose-rich glycoproteins
on pathogens and damaged cells, leading to immune cell activation,
endocytosis, and phagocytosis,
,
but its role in human
milk is not clear.
The loss of these bioactive proteins in HoP-treated
DHM may be
one reason (among other possible factors) for the observed reduced
beneficial impact of DHM as compared with the parent’s own
milk. For example, loss of lactoferrin likely results in reduced protective
effects of milk in infants because the antipathogenic activity of
intact lactoferrin is decreased by HoP processing. Further research
should validate whether these observed protein decreases translate
to health impacts in infants.
3.6
Correlation between Protein Stability and
Physicochemical Properties
To investigate how protein stability
across HoP and UV–C treatment might be impacted by the physicochemical
properties of each protein, we examined the correlation between the
extent of protein changes after HoP or UV–C treatments (Manhattan
distances) and (1) amino acid length, (2) amino acid compositions
(F, Y and W only), (3) hydrophobicity (based on GRAVY score), and
(4) isoelectric point (pI) of each identified protein (each value
in
Supporting Table 2
). Manhattan distances
for each protein in HoP and UV–C samples in comparison with
those in the Raw sample were calculated from the volcano plots in
Section
(
Supporting Tables 3−5
).
UV–C
radiation (230–300 nm)-induced photooxidation has been shown
to cause changes in the primary structure of proteins, including aromatic
amino acids tryptophan, tyrosine, and phenylalanine.
,
Though the UV–C wavelength used herein (254 nm) is a narrower
range, we hypothesized that proteins with high contents of photosensitive
amino acid residues (tryptophan, tyrosine, and phenylalanine) would
be more susceptible to degradation under UV–C treatment. However,
we found no correlations between the percentage of total amino acids
in a protein that were F, Y, or W and the degree of protein change
induced by either UV–C or HoP (
Figure
a). We also found poor correlations between
the degree of protein decrease (based on Manhattan distances) and
other physicochemical properties, including the number of amino acids,
protein hydrophobicity (based on GRAVY score), and protein pI for
both HoP (
R
= −0.016 to 0.130) and UV–C
treatment (
R
= −0.027 to 0.048) (
Figure
b–d). These
results indicated that the physicochemical properties tested in isolation
could not account for which proteins were degraded in HoP or UV–C.

3.7
Comparison of UV–C Dose Effects on
Protein Profile
Human milk protein profiles derived from
DHM samples treated by UV–C at 2000–11,000 J/L were
compared to investigate whether there were any dose effects of UV–C
treatment on human milk proteins. Protein counts ranged from 225 to
240, and remained relatively stable across dosages (i.e., no overall
decrease in counts with increasing dose;
Supporting Table 1
). The sum of abundances of total proteins did not significantly
differ across UV–C treatments (
Supporting Figure 3a
). DHM proteome changes across UV–C treatment

3.8
Strengths, Limitations, and Future Perspectives
This study has numerous strengths. We were able to demonstrate
that proteins identified in UV–C (at 6000 J/L dose)-treated
samples were much more similar to raw human milk in terms of protein
counts, abundances, and bioactivity prediction than HoP samples. Most
human milk proteins were stable during UV–C treatment, whereas
many were degraded by HoP. The observed improved preservation of bioactive
proteins with UV–C compared with HoP enhances the need for
future studies examining the impact of UV–C processing compared
with HoP for DHM on infant health outcomes. These results may contribute
to improving human milk processing methods, which could enhance the
health of infants fed DHM.
A limitation of this study is that
we used a single pool of donor human milk with processing replicates
to assess the impact of the treatment. It is possible that the effect
of treatment could vary depending on the composition of the donor
human milk. Future studies should examine the impacts of these processes
on a larger array of donor milk samples. Future studies should also
compare the impact on the human milk proteome between UV–C
processing and other alternative processing methods, such as high-pressure
processing and high-temperature short-time pasteurization.
Currently,
UV–C systems have not been implemented in milk
banks. Implementation of this process would require the development
of systems scaled to milk bank volume needs. Future studies should
examine the scaling and implementation of UV–C systems at the
human milk bank. Future studies should also examine the impact of
the observed improved preservation of proteins with UV–C compared
to HoP herein on the functionality of milk proteins within the infant
gut and on overall infant health outcomes.
